title: L.A. mayor calls for Casey Wasserman to step down from 2028 Olympics committee
content:
Los Angeles mayor Karen Bass has urged Casey Wasserman to resign as head of the committee overseeing the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games over ties to Ghislaine Maxwell, co-conspirator of convicted sex offender and disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein.

“I cannot fire him,” Bass said in an interview with CNN’s Dana Bass. “My opinion is that he should step down. That’s not the opinion of the board.”

LA28 board’s executive committee last week gave Wasserman a vote of confidence, saying in a statement that after reviewing Wasserman’s interactions with Epstein and Maxwell, it concluded Wasserman “should continue to lead LA28 and deliver a safe and successful Games.”

“The board made a decision. I think that decision was unfortunate. I don’t support the decision. I do think that we need to look at the leadership,” said Bass, who has served as L.A. mayor since 2022. “However, my job as mayor of Los Angeles is to make sure that our city is prepared to have the best Olympics that has ever happened in Olympic history.”

The U.S. Justice Department recently released more than 3 million documents related to Epstein, who pleaded guilty to charges of procuring a child for prostitution in 2008 and died by suicide while in custody on sex trafficking charges in 2019. Wasserman’s name appears in two emails from 2003 with Maxwell, who is now serving a 20-year prison sentence on sex trafficking charges.

Wasserman has maintained he had no contact with Maxwell or Epstein in the past 20 years, but said he deeply regrets his correspondence with Maxwell, “which took place over two decades ago, long before her horrific crimes came to light.”

Bass’ comments come days after Wasserman, 51, announced he would sell his interests in the Wasserman sports and entertainment talent agency, of which he is the founder and CEO.

Several high-profile clients of Wasserman’s, including singer Chappell Roan and retired U.S. soccer star Abby Wambach, announced they’d left the agency in light of the released documents.

“I’m deeply sorry that my past personal mistakes have caused you so much discomfort,” Wasserman wrote in a memo to his employees. “It’s not fair to you, and it’s not fair to the clients and partners we represent so vigorously and care so deeply about.”
